query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A two‐phase coexistence simulation method enhanced with machine‐learning interatomic potentials can replicate the melting properties (melting temperature, fusion entropy and enthalpy, and volume change at melting) of high‐melting refractory materials with nearly DFT-level accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost required by full thermodynamic integration.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐melting refractory material in its crystalline state (e.g., a BCC refractory high‐entropy alloy such as MoNbTaW) with a prepared two‐phase configuration (coexisting solid and liquid regions).
generation.intervention: Implement a two-phase coexistence simulation using an ML-derived interatomic potential calibrated to DFT data.
generation.conditions: Simulations conducted in a controlled temperature ramp near the expected melting point under fixed pressure (or volume) conditions, ensuring thermodynamic equilibrium between the solid and liquid phases.
generation.structural_mediator: The solid-liquid interface, whose dynamics and equilibrium position mediate the determination of melting properties.
generation.mechanism: By directly simulating solid and liquid coexistence, the method extracts the melting temperature from the equilibrium state. Simultaneous analysis of energy and volume changes across the interface enables calculation of enthalpy and entropy of fusion and volume change at melting, all while bypassing the extensive thermodynamic integration over incremental states required in standard ab initio methods.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method will yield melting property values that closely match those obtained from full ab initio free-energy integration, while reducing computational cost significantly, enabling high-throughput screening of refractory materials.
generation.baseline: Ab initio free-energy calculations using DFT-based thermodynamic integration with molecular dynamics.
generation.boundary: Accuracy may be limited for systems with complex microstructures or when the ML potential lacks adequate training for extreme conditions; deviations might occur if interface effects or phase boundary kinetics are not accurately captured.
generation.uncertainty: The transferability and precision of the machine-learning potential in diverse high-temperature regimes remain to be fully validated, especially when compared to traditional DFT approaches.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel simulations on a refractory high-entropy alloy using both the proposed two-phase coexistence method with a machine-learning potential and the traditional ab initio free-energy integration approach. Compare the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting from both methods.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the two-phase coexistence method yields melting property estimates that deviate by more than an acceptable margin (e.g., >10% error relative to ab initio results) or fails to reduce computational cost significantly, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems [24] , [44] – [46] . decision.trend: Initially, the field achieved high accuracy in predicting melting properties by using fully ab initio free‐energy methods based on density functional theory with thermodynamic integration using molecular dynamics. Although these ab initio methods are very reliable, their steep computational cost has hindered their deployment in high‐throughput applications, especially for high‐melting refractory materials. More recently, researchers have begun to adopt advanced sampling techniques and have started employing machine‐learning based interatomic potentials that capture ab initio accuracy while significantly boosting computational efficiency. This trend—from brute‐force thermodynamic integration towards smarter sampling approaches and data‐driven free energy calculations—addresses the need to predict thermodynamic quantities (e.g. melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change upon melting) in settings where direct measurements or full ab initio calculations are too expensive.
decision.unsolved: The core challenge remains the lack of a robust, computationally efficient method that retains DFT-level accuracy for predicting all melting properties in high-temperature materials. The question is how to bypass the extensive thermodynamic integration cost while still resolving key quantities like melting temperature, fusion entropy/enthalpy, and volume change accurately.
decision.lever: Implement a two-phase coexistence simulation method—possibly enhanced with accelerated sampling techniques or coupled with machine-learning derived free energy surfaces—in order to determine melting parameters directly.
decision.why: This approach follows naturally from the trend of reducing the reliance on expensive ab initio MD. By directly simulating a system where both solid and liquid phases coexist, the melting point and associated fusion properties can be extracted with lower computational overhead, making it feasible for high-throughput screening of refractory materials while retaining high accuracy.
